transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2025-11-18
- Time: 15:00 PST
- Duration: ~75 minutes
- Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Liu (Redwood SE), Priya Desai (Redwood Platform), Carlos Mendez (Horizon, Head of ML), Asha Rao (Horizon, Platform Eng), Ben Turner (Horizon, SRE)

Summary:
Quick technical deep dive to align on benchmark methodology for Horizon's on-prem and VPC validation: apples-to-apples comparisons between Redwood Dedicated/Private and Horizon's self-hosted baseline, focusing on latency/throughput, KV cache effects, batching strategies, and quantization impacts. Agree to share harness, prompt sets, and schedule a validation run.

Topics covered:
- Measurement targets: p50/p95/p99 tail latency, tokens/sec, GPU utilization, memory, cold vs warm cache, startup throughput
- Prompt set construction and token distribution (short chatty prompts vs long context completion)
- Load generation: sustained qps vs spikes, open-loop vs closed-loop drivers, replay fidelity
- Quantization methodology and how to keep comparisons fair (same model weights, quantize deterministically, measure quality regression)
- KV cache warmup and cache hit ratios, implications for batching and routing
- VPC/on-prem constraints: network egress, KMS, SOC2 evidence, IAM for test env

Action items (from call):
- Redwood: provide benchmark harness (containerized), load scripts, and sample dashboards
- Horizon: share representative prompt sets and token distribution histograms
- Both: agree on apples-to-apples rules (same model weights, same sequence lengths, identical tokenization)

Transcript:
00:00 - Maya: okay good afternoon everyone, thanks for joining. quick intros from our side — i'm maya, ae for redwood, we have ethan and priya from the runtime team.
00:14 - Carlos: hey thanks, carlos here, uh head of ml at horizon. we mostly want to validate perf on our on-prem infra and then compare to redwood private before we commit to dedicated pools.
00:28 - Ethan: great, can you give a sense of your workloads — is it chat-like short prompts or long generation? that drives batching and kv cache behavior.
00:42 - Carlos: it's mixed. about 60% chat (short), 30% contextual completions with 1–2k context, and some long-form distillations at 8k. token distribution we can share.
00:56 - Asha: also note we have strict p95 SLOs for interactive features, need tail latency < 300ms for most flows.
01:10 - Maya: perfect, that's super helpful. today's goal — align on methodology so when we run benchmarks we're comparing apples to apples. we'll go through prompt sets, load generation approach, what to measure, and how to handle quantization and kv cache.
01:30 - Ben: quick infra note — our on-prem clusters are 8x A100-ish, single tenant, and we have a VPC setup for private deployment tests. curious about network overhead for private control plane.
01:44 - Priya: for the private flow, network control plane traffic is minimal — it's mostly model weights and health checks, while inference stays in your VPC, but we will share exact numbers and egress char to confirm. sometimes people conflate control-plane calls with per-request egress which is not the case.
02:02 - Ethan: ok starting with prompts — we recommend three canonical sets: (1) short-chat (~10–50 tokens), (2) medium-context completions (~200–800 tokens), (3) long-context workloads (2k+). each should include measured token distribution, character-level variability, and failure cases.
02:20 - Carlos: can we also add a 'prefix-heavy' set to exercise kv cache warm hits? some flows repeatedly expand on the same prefix.
02:28 - Ethan: yes that's important; kv cache warmup dramatically changes latency/throughput; we'll include warm/cold variants.
02:40 - Maya: for apples-to-apples, rule one: same base model weights — no model family changes. rule two: deterministic tokenization and seed for generation when measuring latency. rule three: quantization should be applied in a controlled way and reported with exact flags.
02:56 - Carlos: about quantization, our baseline wants int8 4-bit experimentation; how do you ensure quality doesn't diverge? we care about correctness metrics.
03:10 - Priya: we run regression evals tied to prompt sets — BLEU/ROUGE-ish or embedding similarity tests — and threshold T that you accept. Also we can run an A/B test for hallucination rates on your eval set.
03:26 - Asha: and what about kernel selection and compilation differences? our infra uses a different CUDA and compiler stack which might change perf.
03:38 - Ethan: great point; we try to capture the full stack: CUDA/cuDNN versions, kernel lib versions, and any fused-kernel flags. for reproducibility we'll share an environment manifest. if there are compiler-level differences we'll annotate them and try to normalize where possible.
03:56 - Ben: load generation: what's the recommended driver? we've used wrk and a custom go-based harness, but need closed-loop to emulate real clients.
04:10 - Ethan: our harness supports both open-loop (constant QPS) and closed-loop (concurrency-limited) modes. for interactive SLOs closed-loop is more realistic because it respects latency backpressure. open-loop is useful for saturation curves. we'll give you both.
04:28 - Carlos: ok and metrics — we want p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, GPU util, mem, and breakdowns of time spent in attention vs kv cache lookup vs kernel launch. is that feasible?
04:42 - Priya: yes we can instrument per-step time and export trace spans. we can also provide flamegraphs for hot kernels and kv cache hit latency distribution.
04:56 - Maya: early note on kv cache: there are two dimensions — prefix reuse hit rate and per-request sequence length. high cache hit rate can drastically reduce token compute and change batching behavior; so if your workload has heavy prefix reuse, you should run both 'cold' and 'steady-state warm' benchmarks.
05:18 - Carlos: how long to warm the cache? we normally see 30–50 unique prefixes for a user session, but at scale how to simulate?
05:30 - Ethan: we recommend a ramp period in the load generator where repeated prefixes are replayed for a dataset until hit-rate stabilizes; we'll provide a script to calculate observed hit ratio over time. typical warm window is a few minutes depending on your concurrency.
05:46 - Ben: what about batching? i worry batching increases latency for short prompts; but if you cap batch wait time you can trade throughput for tail latency.
05:58 - Priya: exactly — we will test multiple batching configs: no-batching, micro-batching (e.g., 8–16ms wait windows), and larger batch sizes. we'll record tradeoffs: tokens/sec vs p95 tail. also measure cost per token.
06:14 - Carlos: quantify cost for us — we need to pick Dedicated vs build ourselves. how do we make the case?
06:25 - Maya: cost equation is tokens/sec * $gpu-hour + infra overhead + ops. Redwood provides recommendations to minimize unit cost — batching, caching, quantization — but we will produce a cost model for your real traffic profiles.
06:36 - Asha: on VPC/on-prem, PKI and KMS is critical. we need to ensure keys never leave our HSM. can Redwood support customer-managed KMS?
06:46 - Priya: yes we support KM integration and HSM-backed keys for model encryption and audit logs. we'll include docs and an architecture diagram.
06:56 - Ethan: circling back to quantization apples-to-apples: we need to keep the same float32 checkpoints and apply quantization post hoc with the same toolchain. we'll provide the quantize flags and scripts. when measuring quality we'll include embedding-sim and end-user metrics.
07:12 - Carlos: any gotchas with 4-bit quantization and KV cache? we've seen some mismatch with attention scores causing divergence in long contexts.
07:24 - Ethan: that happens — low-bit quant can amplify numerical drift across steps. recommended approach: run mixed precision evals, and if divergence is detected use a hybrid strategy (keep KV cache in higher precision or use per-layer quantization). we'll test hybrid configs.
07:40 - Maya: let's talk about benchmark report layout — we recommend: workload description, environment manifest, raw latency/throughput curves, warm vs cold cache, quantization quality regression table, cost model, and recommended config for your SLOs.
07:56 - Carlos: timeline? we'd like a pilot next week, and on-prem validation the week after.
08:06 - Maya: sounds doable. we'll send the harness today, you send prompts and infra creds for the VPC test by Friday, and we target an on-prem run week of 11/24.
08:18 - Ben: small network question — when running private, do we stream tokens or chunk? how does that affect tail?
08:28 - Priya: we support streaming and chunked responses. streaming slightly increases per-token overhead but reduces perceived latency because first token returns faster. we'll instrument both.
08:40 - Asha: regarding telemetry, we need audit logs per request for compliance — will redwood include that in private?
08:50 - Maya: yes audit logs available and we can increase retention as an add-on. we'll include sample logs in the pack.
09:00 - Carlos: competitor question — we've benchmarked ModelServeX and saw lower p50 but worse p99. what's your approach to tail-focused performance?
09:12 - Ethan: tail performance is about avoiding head-of-line blocking and keeping batch windows adaptive. our routing policy and autoscaling thresholds avoid long queues; we'll show tracing where we reduce p99 by using micro-batches and greedy routing.
09:28 - Maya: ok quick demo plan — ethan will walk through harness and typical output, priya will show kv cache instrumentation.
09:38 - Ethan: opening screen share — (link to harness repo) — note the harness supports variable token payloads, concurrency profiles, and records per-request spans.
10:02 - Ethan: here's a sample run — p50 45ms, p95 210ms, p99 420ms for the short-chat set with micro-batching 12ms wait and kv-warm scenario. these numbers are illustrative; your infra will differ.
10:28 - Carlos: those p99 numbers for warm-cache look promising, but in cold cache we see p99 spike to 1.2s — do you have warmup recommendations?
10:40 - Priya: prefetching prefixes and caching at the edge helps; also using a tiny local LRU for first-hop prefix resolution can mask cold misses. we'll include a warmup script.
10:56 - Ben: logging and instrumentation — we need logs to correlate request IDs with backend spans. how do we propagate IDs?
11:08 - Ethan: the harness injects request IDs and propagates them into spans; we'll share the trace sampling config.
11:18 - Asha: on the security docs, we need SOC2 evidence and network diagrams for our security review.
11:28 - Maya: we'll attach SOC2 report and architecture diagram.
11:36 - Carlos: great. last, let's define acceptance criteria for the pilot — if redwood private meets p95 < 300ms on short-chat and cost per 1M tokens is below X, we move to PoC procurement.
11:52 - Maya: we'll aim to quantify cost with your token mix and provide a recommended config.
12:02 - Carlos: thanks everyone, useful session.
12:12 - Maya: recap of next steps — we'll share harness, security pack, and schedule the on-prem run. Ethan, priya, anything to add?
12:22 - Ethan: i'll push the harness and a sample dashboard by EOD.
12:26 - Priya: i'll assemble the kv-cache instrumentation docs and the KMS integration notes.
12:30 - Maya: Carlos, can you send the prompt sets by Friday?
12:34 - Carlos: yes will do.
12:38 - Maya: awesome, we'll follow up in email with links and calendar invites. thanks all!
